newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ready for four more years.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ready for four more years.

text.p: President Bill Clinton takes the oath of office to start his second term on Monday, hoping his final four years in the White House will be marked by political healing instead of the partisan blood-sport that has so far made his presidency a wild roller coaster ride.

Thousands of loyal Democrats and just plain tourists have poured into town to turn the 20th century's last presidential inauguration into a gala party and honour a man who only two years ago, was so far down in the polls that he gave a speech pleading that he was still relevant.

The inaugural parade route down Pennsylvania Avenue, from the halls of Congress to the White House, has been spruced up and decked with flags, bunting and bandstands -- some of which have equipped with bullet-proof glass to protect VIPs.

As Clinton prepares to be sworn in, a New York Times/CBS poll published on Monday showed the 50-year-old Arkansan entering his second term with a 60 percent approval rating and with two-thirds of the country saying they were optimistic that his second term would be a success.

Rather than just bask in the glory of being the first Democrat to be re-elected since the Second World War, Clinton seemed eager to make his second inaugural address a serious appeal for both political and racial healing after the chief justice of the United States, William Reinquist, administers the 35-word oath of office.

While his speech has been kept secret, there were plenty of hints over the weekend that the American public was fed up with politics as usual and that he wants to lead the charge for change and secure his place in history.

"I hope that I can set a tone on Monday and in the days ahead that will help flush the poison out of the atmosphere and get people to thinking about the folks that sent us here," he told the Washington Post in an interview on Sunday.

Clinton, whose first term was marred by numerous, ongoing probes into his business, political and private life, said politicians were devoting too much time investigating alleged scandals that took a huge amount of emotional energy from all involved.
"All of us, we have so little time and it passes so fast and we can do so much when we work together and think about the interests of the people and the future," he said.

In a number of interviews he gave over the weekend, Clinton stressed that he wanted a balanced budget agreement that would pave the way for refinancing Social Security and Medicare, the most complicated domestic issues facing him in his next term.
Under fire for the Democratic Party's acceptance of millions of dollars in improper campaign contributions from foreigners, Clinton also promised a major bi-partisan effort at reform.

White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles told NBC television's "Meet the Press" programme that Clinton will also talk about "how the American people need to come together on common ground. I think before this president came to office, there was a real effort ... to divide this country on wedge issues along racial, along ethnic and religious grounds."

The president, first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and their daughter Chelsea took time off from the inaugural preparations on Sunday to attend a sometimes fawning show business tribute at a sports stadium featuring such stars as Whoopi Goldberg, Michael Douglas, Aretha Franklin, Stevie Wonder, James Taylor, Mikhail Baryshnikov, Yo Yo Ma, Kenny Rogers and Kenny G.

A crowd of 13,000 men in tuxedos and women in ball gowns and fur coats paid up to $3,000 a ticket for the chance to munch on pretzels and hot dogs and hear Goldberg address the president as "Bill" and declare, "It is amazing to see a friend, who is truly a friend, inaugurated as president of the United States. They (the Clinton family) are three of the coolest people I know."

Women at the gala were advised to put their fur coats under their seats so they would not be seen on television and thus irritate anti-fur activists. "It wouldn't be politically correct," an usher said.

When it was Clinton's turn to speak, the theme of the looming inauguration popped up. "Tomorrow we will not just celebrate our democracy, we must renew it. Tomorrow we'll be preparing our nation for a brand new century and a brand new millenium with brand new adventures and mountains to climb for all future generations of Americans," he said.
